If your recording only expands to a few hours, then you need to consider reducing that threshold to get the data for that specific day.

Jairo

Hi again,

Now you can test a solution I implemented for this.

1. Install version with the fix:
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("wadpac/GGIR", ref = "issue1265_onlyOneMetric")

2. Run GGIR again, and make sure you include the following parameters as they are here:
GGIR(
     mode = 1:4,
     datadir = "yourPath2datadir",
     outputdir = "yourPath2outputdir",
     dataFormat = "actiwatch_csv",
     extEpochData_timeformat = "%Y-%m-%d %I:%M:%S %p",
     windowsizes = c(120,600,1800),
     do.zcy = TRUE, do.enmo = FALSE, do.anglez = FALSE,
     acc.metric = "ZCY",
     HASIB.algo = "Sadeh1994",
     def.noc.sleep = c(),
     mvpadur = c(2, 5, 10),
     boutdur.mvpa = c(6, 10),
     boutdur.lig = c(6, 10)
  )

Main changes to your script:
Metrics definition: make sure to only calculate zcy, which is the metric we assume it was calculated by the actiwatch (more info here). So turn off calculation of enmo and anglez (this is not problematic but will prevent you from receiving some warnings). Same for acc.metric, make sure it is "ZCY".
Bout durations: the error you were getting was related to detection of bouts, GGIR cannot calculate bouts of 1 minute if the epoch length is 2 minutes, then the calculation failed. Additionally, make sure that mvpadur is a vector of length 3 as required by GGIR part 2
What to expect:
In the file that you provided, almost the full recording is 0 count epochs, meaning that GGIR cannot detect any sleep period, and therefore only part 2 output would be generated (not part 4 or 5), therefore, make sure you do not include 5 in the definition of mode.

Please, let us know if this worked out for you.

Best,
Jairo

messages.subject: Re: Part 2 vs Part 5 output
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

In part 2, GGIR uses includedaycrit to define valid days, which requires a minimum number of hours per calendar day.

In part 5, GGIR uses includedaycrit.part5, which only looks at the number of valid hours during the awake time classified in that specific day.

Also, the timewindow definition in part 5 ("MM", "WW", "OO") can make the number of valid days inconsistent between parts 2 and 5.

Best,
Jairo

messages.body_plain:
Hi Zachary,

SRI in GGIR is derived from the detected rest periods (sustained inactivity bouts) and does not discriminate specifically between the main sleep window and naps. I used this approach because we do not have a robust nap detection method yet.

However, I have recently corresponded about this with Andrew Phillips (who originally proposed SRI) and I am now planning to make a few updates in the upcoming months:

I will add functionality to make SRI more compatible with their approach.
I plan to update the GGIR documentation on SRI to better clarify the differences.

Thanks,

Vincent

Dear Vincent,

I noticed that W0.5 is consistently 1 for all 1080 participants, suggesting that the issue is not related to the input data. Instead, I believe the unexpected results are related to the definition of xmin.

In the g.fragmentation function, xmin is set to 1 (GGIR/R/g.fragmentation.R at master · wadpac/GGIR · GitHub <https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/blob/master/R/g.fragmentation.R#L4> line 4), which makes sense, as 1 (i.e., 5s) is the shortest recordable (though not necessarily observed) bout length. However, in the g.part5_analyseSegment function, xmin is overwritten as 60/ws3new, resulting in a value of 12 (60/5) (GGIR/R/g.part5_analyseSegment.R at master · wadpac/GGIR · GitHub <https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/blob/master/R/g.part5_analyseSegment.R#L398> line 398).

This adjustment appears to cause the very low results for alpha and the median bout length, leading to a proportion of 1 for all participants. When setting xmin to 1, the results seem more realistic.

Was there a specific reason for defining xmin as 12 in this case?

I appreciate your insights.

Best regards,

Anne

messages.subject: MIMS as an external function
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

As has been discussed previously, GGIR does not currently have a way to automatically calculate MIMS units directly within a normal GGIR function call. As such, it seemed like a sensible temporary solution to set up the MIMSunit package function as an external function provided to GGIR. The process of doing this is straightforward thanks to great documentation and examples on the github page (thanks Vincent and others!).

To facilitate this as an easily accessible path for other users who might be interested in doing the same such that MIMS can be calculated with some standardization to other metrics (e.g., the handling of nonwear time for ENMO calculations), I put together a very simple Rmarkdown file (see attached html) describing the process. In testing so far it seems to provide reasonable estimates.

Before putting this out there as an Rpub document that others might use, I am hoping to check whether there is anything obviously egregious that makes the external function approach invalid for MIMS regarding the way data are internally handled. If so I would really like to avoid leading others astray! Caveats about speed based on previous conversations are acknowledged. Any other thoughts or suggestions also appreciated.

Thank you for your time and help,
Tom

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom,

Thanks for sharing, I guess this is helpful for some.
Here a my comments:

> Currently, this procedure produces values that are not exactly the same as those produced by running the...

This paragraph invalidates your approach because a new implementation that it is not consistent with the original is problematic in research. Instead, turn off auto-calibration (do.cal = FALSE) and imputation (do.imp=FALSE) and make sure your reference 5 seconds estimates are just like GGIR aligned with the start of a minute. The resulting values should be identical. If not, then I think you cannot recommend this approach to the research community, because there are inconsistencies without explanation. Instead of promoting the method it would then be best to invest the energy in researching the differences.

> It is also important to note that the issue of calculating MIMS from within GGIR is not new, and has previously received attention from developers of both groups (s

I would like to propose removing the last paragraph and replacing it with a call for researchers to find funding to speed up the MIMSunit package, because that is ultimately the best solution for the community. It allows us to embed MIMSunit as a dependency of GGIR such that we no longer need this external function solution and it makes it easier for anyone using R to work with MIMSunit. The discussion I had with the MIMSunit was just a discussion and I would be really worried if researchers started using these code snippets I shared without doing further research first. I am concerned that it will lead to unnecessary methodological inconsistencies.

Best,

Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent,

My sincere thank you for your thoughtful comments. Of course that's a great idea to set do.cal and do.imp = FALSE, I don't know why that didn't occur to me. When doing so, the MIMS output is nearly identical to the original but with some very minor differences. In attempting to dig deeply into this, I can see with a breakpoint within my external function that the raw acceleration values being used in the external function are not quite the same as those that are used when reading the data in directly with GGIRread (readAxivity() ). These differences in the acceleration data appear to account for the differences that I am seeing in the final products.

This surprised me given that imputation and auto-calibration should be disabled. So I figured that this could be due to some other potential candidate settings, which I configured as follows:
"GGIR(...,
nonWearEdgeCorrection = F,
ignorenonwear=F,
spherecrit=0,
interpolationType=1,
frequency_tol=0.1,
backup.cal.coef = "redo")"

As I would have originally expected, none of these parameters made a difference: the acceleration values used at the time of the external function are still not the same at relevant timepoints as those that come from a readAxivity() of the raw .cwa file.

My next suspicion was that the difference was coming from the resampling procedure that occurs here in the GGIR codebase: https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/blob/19a8c42009a8315f89c3f2a8956619d7d3400648/R/g.readaccfile.R#L248
However, after a thorough inspection, the resampling procedure also does not appear to account for any of the differences in the acceleration data that I am noting at the time of external function application.

So, I am wondering if you could point me towards any other place in GGIR that would transform the acceleration data prior to application of an external function? I have searched elsewhere in the list of parameters and traced the processing steps in the code base for Axivity files, but haven't been able to find any other good candidates.

Finally, regarding your last point, I agree wholeheartedly and will change the document accordingly. As a side note, my own tweaks to speed up mims_unit without changing outcomes at all (mainly through improved vectorization) have only managed to reduce runtimes by a meager ~3%... my suspicion is that in order to keep the entire original MIMS algorithm, the best bet may be to move computationally intensive parts to C++ via Rcpp. Something I hope to delve into in the future, though perhaps a fool's errand?

Thank you,
Tom

I am now able to perfectly reproduce mims_unit() outcomes when running as an external function through GGIR. Notably, GGIR versus the use of readAxivity() output fed directly into mims_unit() were handling a boundary point differently occuring right near the starttime, leading to some non-alignment in binning between the two approaches (e.g., a numeric value with something like 1653961499.999197959).

messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] Is Imputation Possible Only in Middle (Not Ends) of Collection Period?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joanna,

GGIR facilitates masking segments of the recordings based on your study protocol as you already discovered: https://wadpac.github.io/GGIR/articles/chapter5_StudyProtocol.html

The masked periods are always imputed. This is needed in case any part of them ends up being used as part of a valid recording day. For example, if you only mask the first 2 hours of the first day then that day may still be valid, but we need those first 2 hours imputed. However, when large parts or even entire days are considered invalid then those are excluded from all csv reports, so for those days it does not matter whether we impute or not.

The only place where you will still see those imputed days of data is in the visual reports, which intentionally show the entire original time series to avoid any misunderstanding about the duration of a recording.

If it is important to you that visual report show non-imputed data for invalid days then I am happy to develop that as part of a paid consultancy. Please pm me if you are interested.

Best,

Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marcello,

As far as I know (but could be wrong of course), there is not a pre-packaged way to do this with the external function parameter settings.However, you could easily make a minor customization to allow this.

The good news is that the external function (applyExtFunction.R is the relevant script) is already provided initially with data that includes the temperature data for your device. However, basically the first operation performed removes everything except for the acceleration columns. You can see that line of code here: https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/blob/40869c8754bb0c06913b57c1709c9c1197c3ccbe/R/applyExtFunction.R#L2

So my approach would be to add a logical parameter to `applyExtFunction` called something like "include.temp". Then modify the applyExtFunction to include a 4th column in the the data matrix for temperature if include.temp == T. Note that to do this you also have to modify the function "check_myfun.R" because it is programmed to search for unexpected parameters and throw an error if there's an issue.

These minor modifications could be incorporated into GGIR, but if I had to guess there is probably a reason that this is a bad idea (though unless the include.temp parameter is set, it wouldn't break anything...).

In case it's helpful I included two modified script files that overwrite the GGIR package functions making the suggested changes. Hope this helps,

Tom
